item.title: Practical Considerations for Processing Massive Classical Data via Quantum Oracle Sketching
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — DNA retrieval accuracy reaches >0.98 with M0=2048 samples per oracle across Q=8 applications out of 16288 corpus windows, scaling in relative error as EF(Q)∝Q2/M. Transpiled circuits remain deep, exceeding 4.17×105 depth even after phase fusion.

Grade 0.414 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Stefano Markidis

Figure

Fingerprint matrix relative error EF(Q) and mean top-one DNA family-retrieval accuracy as functions of total sample count M across different oracle repetition counts Q.

Asks

What are the practical system and compilation requirements for implementing Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) on current batched quantum hardware?

But

Offline simulation only; transpiled circuits require hundreds of thousands of CX gates, exceeding current NISQ coherence times.

Tools

Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) · Offline phase fusion compilation · Qiskit transpiler (GenericBackendV2) · DNA sequence fingerprinting

Abstract

Classical-to-quantum I/O is a critical bottleneck for data-intensive quantum workloads. Quantum Oracle Sketching (QOS) has been proposed to address this problem. We identify its practical requirements, including the representation of data as a probability distribution over oracle addresses, the relation between sample count, approximation error, and update cost, and the coherence and runtime support required for online execution. To study QOS on current quantum computing devices, we develop an offline realization that compiles sample blocks into empirical phase oracles and evaluate it using DNA fingerprinting. The application converges with relatively few samples, while exact phase fusion combines repeated updates to the same address. However, the compiled circuits remain too deep for current quantum computing devices. Practical QOS therefore requires lower depth oracle synthesis and interactive quantum runtimes.

item.title: OpenQARP: a modular framework for quantum application research
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — OpenQARP executes operator algebra one to two orders of magnitude faster than OpenFermion and matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count while keeping strict unified conventions.

Grade 0.406 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Stefano Scali, Vicente P. Soloviev, Antonio Márquez Romero, Brian Coyle, Giuseppe Buonaiuto, Annie Paine, Jonathan H. Fetherolf, Marcos Diez García, Michal Krompiec, Josh Kirsopp

Figure

Run-phase simulation time on a logarithmic vertical axis plotted against register size for brickwork circuits, comparing constant-factor scaling across different quantum simulation frameworks.

Asks

How to build an open-source quantum computing framework that eliminates silent convention errors across the research workflow while maintaining high simulator and operator performance?

Before

OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket required cross-framework plumbing with differing qubit orderings and phase conventions.

But

Benchmarks measured on a single Apple-silicon host using scalar C++ block kernels without SIMD or AVX vectorization; no pulse-level control, autodiff, or direct hardware execution engine.

Tools

C++20 compiled core with Python interface · block-based circuit abstraction · gate fusion and flip-mask Pauli contraction · independent NumPy/SciPy testing oracles

Code. https://github.com/OpenQARP/openqarp

Abstract

We introduce OpenQARP, the Open Quantum Application Research Package: an open-source Python framework for quantum application research, built on a compiled C++ core. In OpenQARP, an application is assembled from an algorithm library that orchestrates three interchangeable layers: blocks describe circuits, primitives describe what to extract from them, and engines describe how they run. The release spans near-term through fault-tolerant methods, targeting problems from electronic structure to combinatorial optimization, with device-aware compilation, circuit cutting, and resource estimation over a single set of numerical conventions that the code must follow. Every numerical feature is checked against an independent oracle, and every published timing carries a correctness check. Against OpenFermion, Qiskit/Aer, PennyLane/Lightning, Qulacs, qsim, and pytket, OpenQARP is one to two orders of magnitude faster on operator algebra and among the fastest on simulation. It matches mature compilers on two-qubit gate count, and expresses a complete algorithm in the lines a framework needs rather than the plumbing a primitive stack demands.

item.title: Efficient expectation value estimation for quantum circuits via extended stabilizer frameworks and adaptive variance estimation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Estimates quantum circuit expectation values by merging sum-over-Clifford with quasiprobability stabilizer simulation and adaptive variance stopping, reducing sample complexity dependence on gate-wise stabilizer extent from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime.

Grade 0.384 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Yunseo Hwang, Giwon Song, Kyoung Keun Park, Hyukjoon Kwon, Taehyun Kim

Asks

Can classical estimation of observable expectation values for non-Clifford quantum circuits bypass conservative Hoeffding-bound sampling overheads without extra space complexity?

Before

Standard quasiprobability stabilizer decompositions scale quadratically with stabilizer extent using worst-case Hoeffding bounds.

But

Advantage over standard scaling relies on low-variance regime; restricted to expectation value estimation rather than full state sampling.

Tools

sum-over-Clifford method · quasiprobability-based stabilizer simulation · adaptive empirical variance estimation

Abstract

Classical simulability of quantum circuits plays a central role in characterizing and quantifying quantum computational advantage. Typically, the presence of non-Clifford gates introduces an exponential runtime overhead for classically estimating expectation values of observables. In this work, we introduce an efficient simulation framework that integrates the sum-over-Clifford method with quasi-probability-based stabilizer simulation to directly estimate expectation values. To optimize efficiency, we incorporate a circuit-adaptive reduction via variance estimation protocol, which terminates simulations once an empirical confidence bound is sufficient to guarantee the prescribed error tolerance. Our method circumvents overly conservative Hoeffding's inequality, thereby reducing the dependence on the gate-wise stabilizer extent from quadratic to linear in the low-variance regime, while maintaining the same space complexity as previous approaches. We explicitly prove the sample-complexity reduction for random quantum circuits and T-doped Clifford circuits and also empirically validate these advantages in the quantum approximate optimization algorithm and quantum kernel method.

item.title: Derivatives of Quantum Randomness: Separating Pseudorandom Unitaries from Pseudorandom (Function-like) States
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Unitary oracle separates pseudorandom function-like state generators (PRFSGs) from pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs). Adaptively secure, quantum-accessible PRFSGs do not imply non-adaptively secure, forward-only PRUs, even for non-unitary implementations with polynomial ancilla space.

Grade 0.383 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “sampling-based quantum advantage and its classical spoofing” · Minki Hhan

Asks

Can pseudorandom function-like state generators be used to construct pseudorandom unitaries when unrestricted ancillary qubits are permitted?

Before

Partial oracle separations existed only for candidate PRU constructions with severely bounded ancilla space.

But

Black-box separation relative to a unitary oracle combined with 𝖰𝖯𝖲𝖯𝖠𝖢𝖤.

Tools

common-Haar function-like state (CHFS) oracle · Poincaré inequalities on sphere products · low-rank gradient analysis · quantum OR test · quantum process tomography

Abstract

Quantum computation gives rise to new pseudorandom primitives for states and unitaries, including pseudorandom state generators (PRSGs), pseudorandom function-like state generators (PRFSGs), and pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs). In this paper, we show a full unitary oracle separation between PRFSGs and PRUs. The separation holds between the strongest state notion and the weakest unitary notion: even adaptively secure, quantum-accessible PRFSGs do not imply non-adaptively secure, forward-only PRUs, even when their implementations are allowed to be non-unitary and use an arbitrary number of ancillary qubits. This reveals a fundamental distinction between pseudorandomness for quantum states and for quantum unitaries. Our main technical idea is to view a candidate PRU construction with access to state generation oracles as a map from the underlying oracle states to implemented unitaries, and to study the derivatives of this map. These derivatives are inherently low rank, and we exploit this low-rank structure to distinguish the resulting unitaries from truly random ones. We believe this differential perspective may be useful for studying other structural questions about quantum states and unitaries.

item.title: A Modular, Topology-Aware Software Stack for Entanglement-Based Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — For an 18-qubit QFT circuit on a 2-QPU network, replacing all-to-all with nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity increases EPR-pair consumption by more than an order of magnitude. Under stochastic link generation, shortest-duration and critical-path arbitration policies reduce completion time by 17.7±1.3% and 17.9±1.5% relative to FIFO.

Grade 0.382 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Luke Andreesen, Shobhit Gupta, Sean Sullivan, Manish Kumar Singh

Figure

EPR-pair consumption (y-axis) for 18-qubit QFT and 64-qubit Adder circuits on a 2-QPU network under all-to-all versus nearest-neighbor intra-QPU connectivity (x-axis) across three partitioning strategies.

Asks

How can hardware network topology and link contention be incorporated into an open-source software stack for partitioning, compiling, and scheduling distributed quantum circuits?

Before

Prior distributed compilers (such as Pytket-DQC) lack timestamped operation scheduling and rely on idealized, optimistic all-to-all connectivity assumptions.

But

NISQ-era compilation only; does not model decoherence, noise, link fidelity degradation, entanglement distillation, or quantum error correction.

Tools

OpenQASM compiler toolchain · Discrete-event stochastic scheduler · Quantum Network Constructor (QNC) · Hypergraph and Dynamic Interaction circuit partitioners · Cat-Entangler and Cat-Disentangler teleportation protocols

Code. https://github.com/memQGit/dqc

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing (DQC) seeks to scale beyond the limits of monolithic processors by interconnecting multiple quantum processing units (QPUs) through entanglement-based links. Realizing this vision requires the co-design of hardware and software across the domains of quantum networking, compilation, and scheduling, yet existing tools remain fragmented between monolithic circuit compilers and long-distance quantum network simulators. We present an open-source, topology-informed framework for the compilation and scheduling of distributed quantum programs. Given an input circuit and a description of the target network, the framework partitions and reconstructs the circuit into a distributed program that respects the specified inter- and intra-QPU topology, covers cross-QPU operations through gate and state teleportation, and schedules the result under either deterministic or stochastic entanglement-generation models. By accepting and emitting standard OpenQASM, the framework interoperates with existing monolithic toolchains, and its standardized module interfaces allow partitioning and scheduling strategies to be interchanged and benchmarked. Using this framework, we show that the best-performing compilation strategy varies across the tested circuits and network configurations, and that both network topology and intra-QPU connectivity substantially affect the entanglement cost of execution. These findings underscore the need for a co-design approach to distributed quantum computing, which our framework is designed to support.

item.title: Variational Real-Time Dynamics on Reduced Operator Manifolds
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) updates parameterized circuits by matching Ehrenfest equations on polynomial-sized operator sets without quantum geometric tensor calculation. Reaches ground-state energy error ∼3×10−3 when generating QSCI subspaces on a 20-qubit simulator and executes on up to 24 superconducting qubits.

Grade 0.378 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Aeishah Ameera Anuar, PV Sriluckshmy, Riccardo Rossi, Fedor Simkovic

Figure

Energy error |E−EFCI| as a function of the cutoff fraction of the configuration interaction subspace size R, comparing exact time evolution to OVQRTE with SPSA gradient estimation across various evolution iterations for a 20-qubit system.

Asks

How can variational real-time dynamics be formulated to avoid measuring the quantum geometric tensor while reducing quantum circuit and measurement costs?

But

Demonstrated for systems up to 24 qubits, tested with Ns=22 SPSA samples per gradient step, requires selected reduced operator manifolds.

Tools

Operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE) · Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) · Quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI) · Low-depth unitary coupled cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) ansatz · IQM Emerald superconducting processor

Abstract

Accurate real-time simulation of correlated quantum systems remains challenging for both classical methods and near-term quantum hardware. We introduce operator-projected variational quantum real-time evolution (OVQRTE), which updates a parameterized circuit by enforcing the Ehrenfest equations for a selected set of observables. OVQRTE requires only expectation-value measurements, while the choice of operator set enables a systematic trade-off between accuracy and measurement cost, substantially reducing quantum-resource requirements relative to existing variational real-time-evolution algorithms. After implementing OVQRTE dynamics of Heisenberg model on a simulator, we benchmark the algorithm for the Anderson impurity models on the IQM Emerald superconducting processor using up to 24 qubits. We further use OVQRTE to sample computational-basis states for quantum-selected configuration interaction (QSCI), enabling the calculation of the ground-state energy and density of states within a self-consistent ghost-Gutzwiller Ansatz (gGut) embedding loop. Our results establish OVQRTE as a promising approach for investigating correlated condensed-matter systems on near-term quantum hardware.

item.title: Quantum Codes for Generalized Amplitude-damping Noise
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) on a five-qubit permutation-invariant code achieves fidelity loss that scales quadratically with generalized amplitude-damping strength γ, O(γ2), under post-selected recovery.

Grade 0.376 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Sourav Dutta, Anubhab Rudra, Manav Seksaria, Anil Prabhakar, Prabha Mandayam

Figure

Entanglement fidelity and recovery probability as functions of damping strength γ at excitation parameter p=0.05. The numerically optimized code achieves higher entanglement fidelity than the [5,1] permutation-invariant code at the cost of lower success probability.

Asks

Can probabilistic and approximate quantum error correction frameworks be combined to suppress first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors in short codes?

Before

Deterministic quantum codes (such as the [5,1,3] stabilizer code) cannot eliminate first-order generalized amplitude-damping errors and incur fidelity loss scaling linearly with γ.

But

Requires post-selection over successful recovery outcomes, reducing total success probability below 1.

Tools

five-qubit permutation-invariant code · probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC) · semidefinite programming · Charnes-Cooper transformation

Abstract

Quantum error correcting (QEC) plays a crucial role in protecting quantum information against decoherence and enabling scalable, reliable quantum computing. One of the most realistic and ubiquitous sources of noise affecting quantum hardware today is generalized amplitude-damping (GAD) noise. Conventional, deterministic QEC codes struggle to correct for GAD noise because of their inherent structure, leading to fidelity losses that scale linearly with the damping strength. In this work, we introduce the framework of probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC), that combines the flexibility of approximate QEC with the potential of post-selected recovery, enabling high-fidelity, resource-efficient error correction. We construct a five-qubit permutation-invariant code that, under probabilistic recovery, achieves a fidelity loss quadratic in the damping strength, thus outperforming existing QEC codes. Formulating PAQEC as an optimization problem, we present a numerical technique based on Charnes-Cooper and semidefinite programming to identify the optimal recovery map for any PAQEC code. Our results establish PAQEC as a powerful tool for developing resource-efficient, high-fidelity quantum codes tailored to realistic noise, with promising implications for near-term quantum devices and future fault-tolerant architectures.

item.arxave:abstract: Quantum error correcting (QEC) plays a crucial role in protecting quantum information against decoherence and enabling scalable, reliable quantum computing. One of the most realistic and ubiquitous sources of noise affecting quantum hardware today is generalized amplitude-damping (GAD) noise. Conventional, deterministic QEC codes struggle to correct for GAD noise because of their inherent structure, leading to fidelity losses that scale linearly with the damping strength. In this work, we introduce the framework of probabilistic approximate quantum error correction (PAQEC), that combines the flexibility of approximate QEC with the potential of post-selected recovery, enabling high-fidelity, resource-efficient error correction. We construct a five-qubit permutation-invariant code that, under probabilistic recovery, achieves a fidelity loss quadratic in the damping strength, thus outperforming existing QEC codes. Formulating PAQEC as an optimization problem, we present a numerical technique based on Charnes-Cooper and semidefinite programming to identify the optimal recovery map for any PAQEC code. Our results establish PAQEC as a powerful tool for developing resource-efficient, high-fidelity quantum codes tailored to realistic noise, with promising implications for near-term quantum devices and future fault-tolerant architectures.

item.title: Disentangling QAOA: From Weakly Entangled Circuits to a Classical QUBO Solver
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Disentangled QAOA projected to product states (bond dimension χ=1) achieves cut ratios above 0.95 relative to best-known values on GSet MaxCut instances up to 20000 variables without per-instance tuning.

Grade 0.376 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Boris I. Bantysh, Andrey Yu. Chernyavskiy, Denis A. Kulikov, Maksim A. Gavreev, Evgeniy O. Kiktenko

Figure

MPS bond dimension χ plotted across normalized circuit layer index ℓ/p for depths p=5 and p=100. Shows an entangle-disentangle profile where peak bond dimension decreases and saturates with increasing depth.

Asks

How much of the optimization power of expanding-depth QAOA survives when circuit entanglement is completely removed?

But

Restricted to the fixed-parameter expanding-depth QAOA regime; not a general claim for all variational quantum optimization or other parameter schedules.

Tools

Fixed-parameter sin-cos QAOA schedule · Matrix product state (MPS) simulation · Product-state projection (χ=1) · Bloch-vector algebraic updates

Abstract

The role of entanglement in quantum optimization remains actively debated. To address this question, we focus on the fixed-parameter expanding-depth regime of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), where a compact two-parameter schedule is trained once on small instances and then applied as the problem size and circuit depth increase. To probe this regime beyond full state-vector simulation, we perform approximate matrix product state simulations for up to 50 qubits and 100 layers and quantify entanglement by the bond dimension. We observe an entangle--disentangle profile, with the peak bond dimension decreasing with depth and eventually saturating. This observation motivates an extreme approximation: projecting the state onto the product-state manifold (bond dimension one) after every two-qubit interaction. Based on this approximation, we introduce BOND-1, a quantum-inspired classical solver. Despite the drastic simplification, BOND-1 achieves cut ratios above 0.95 relative to the best known values on standard GSet MaxCut benchmarks with up to 20000 variables, and in some cases it matches those values. It achieves these results without per-instance optimization and has linear memory cost, while per-instance tuning can provide further improvement. These results show that, in this regime, a substantial fraction of the optimization power of QAOA survives even in the complete absence of entanglement. Our conclusions, however, are specific to this setting and do not imply that entanglement is unnecessary for quantum optimization in general.
